text: Hi, welcome to this session.

text: It is mysteriously titled The Agent Behind the Curtain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's about how the team at Warp build our cloud agent platform.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Before I talk about the how, though, I want to talk about the why and share a little bit about my own background.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I've spent the past eight years building developer tooling.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I started off in open source in the Python and data science space on the Jupyter Notebook core team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I was a maintainer on the Interact project.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That work continued in my time at Microsoft helping build APIs and SDKs for web developers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And now I'm working on bringing AI agents to the cloud at warp.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And one of the lessons that I've learned in my time building developer tooling is that really good dev tools meet devs where they are and grow with them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A tool that you're gonna be using every day should accommodate your workflows but also be really adaptable as the complexity and the nature of the work changes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's important for us to build really great DevTools because DevTools have a compounding effect on the world.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you make a piece of software that helps a developer or a builder do great work, your ability to magnify how much great software exists in the world increases.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I think it is super important that these dev tools accommodate people's workflows.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And people's workflows are important because they love their preferences.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You might have a preference for a shell, a language, a harness, a review process.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And something that adapts to your workflows and preferences is going to be more enjoyable to use and more enjoyable to build software with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it also becomes like a part of how you think and build.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it's super important to be attuned to that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this notion of tools meeting developers where they are and growing with them comes to light really clearly in the progression of AI tooling in this space.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is the story for warp specifically, but it's also the story for a lot of developer tools.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Pre-AI era, we had the warp terminal, which kind of met people in their command line workflows that they were used to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then this fantastic thing happened where AI got introduced to developers, and now you had a whole new set of tools that was available to you locally on your machine.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And a lot of people started to interact with agentic coding patterns in their terminal, in their IDE, in their editor.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then eventually we realized that we had kind of reached the limits of what we could do on our laptops and we wanted agents to do work that was more long running, that was adaptive to different constraints and that work needed to happen in the cloud.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And whenever you send anything to the cloud, you adopt a law of complexity because running things in the cloud requires us to navigate a much messier stack of infrastructure concerns.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when I say we here, I mean the people building developer tools because that is the person that I am.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it gets at one of the things that are like a core principle in how we think about unlocking capabilities here and building good developer tools is that platforms should take on complexity before it reaches the user.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A really good experience should not expose anything of the leaky complexity that it handles to you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When we think about building our cloud agent platform, we try and structure it so that every primitive models this philosophy of hiding complexity from the user so they can focus on the work that matters to them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first place that this shows up when you're building a cloud agent platform is where does the agent run if it's not running on a developer's machine?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It needs a place to do its work like any developer would, and that place is typically a sandbox.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's an isolated environment in the cloud where agents do this task.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When we started building these out for our cloud agent platform, our first situation was to provide self-hosted sandboxes so that developers had a really easy on-ramp for getting into our cloud agent platform.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You didn't have to think about where your compute lived.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It was just there for you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the reality is that for teams doing serious work, they're probably managing their own infrastructure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They probably have dev boxes that they need to interact with.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so something that is hosted or managed is usually not sufficient.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You really need to be able to run agent workloads on infrastructure that people bring so it adapts to their security concerns, their deployment practices, their workflows and preferences on their team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so you add support for not only managed hosting, but also self-hosting to the platform.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that is complexity that you abstract away from the user and how the behavior is modeled.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The next kind of component is a little bit more personal to people, and it's the harness that they want to use.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As we talked about earlier, people are really passionate about the tools that shape their workflows.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One of those tools is the harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Who here has a preference for Claude Code as a harness locally?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Codex, something else entirely, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So much diversity in the room and we want to meet people where they work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you want to integrate multi-harness support that not only accommodates preferences but also gives people the ability to use the right tool for the job.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And flexibility isn't something that should just be crammed into a platform because a real risk you run if you cram it in is that it becomes fragmented.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your experience with working with Claude is different from working with Codex versus a custom harness that you might have.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so one of the key properties is making sure that the platform provides structure and guardrails around the harness so that the experience is consistent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For us, this means that harnesses can interact with all of the platform native experiences.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So just being able to store conversation state and rehydrate it, being able to interact with the artifacts and outputs that are produced by agents, whether they're PRs, issues, new files that are generated.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All of that should kind of be structured the same way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Okay, cool.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we gave you a place for your agent to run, and we gave you a choice for what harness you use, including Warpstone harness and any other harnesses that you want to bring.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What if one agent isn't enough to do work?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's the reality of most software engineering.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I wish that I could just send off one prompt and solve all of the problems that exist in my software, but the reality is that real engineering work rarely fits inside one prompt.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In a typical workflow, you might need one agent to go research a problem and plan a solution.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You might need another agent to implement it, and you might need to bring in a third to validate it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you might want each of these agents to use different harnesses and different models in order to have a real adversarial and robust approach.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we have built-in support for that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can orchestrate agents across the stack.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: With a lot of agent-based experiences, this orchestration happens via a prompt.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I say slash orchestrate or I queue the agent via prompting that I wanted to delegate work across multiple sub-agents for a task that I have here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this orchestrator agent will do all of the messy complexity of interacting with sub-agents, mediating messages between them, and tracking the work that's happening for me behind the scenes with a single prompt.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We abstract complexity away from the user by giving them this experience.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This sort of prompt-based model for interacting with agents and sub-agents is really powerful.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: An even more interesting one is the notion of interacting with agents and sub-agents via the API.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So everything in our surface area is exposed via an API and I can fire off a request to say that I want to run a sub-agent that is attached to a parent agent via configuration that I provide.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this API is super magical because this is the key component of a platform.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's exposing the primitives in a way that users can build on top of.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The thing about great APIs and SDKs is people can build on top of them, which means that they're not restricted to your UI or your opinion of how a particular experience should look.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is where like composability becomes really powerful.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so we're trying to be intentional about exposing an API for every key component of the stack.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is APIs for spinning up agents and sub-agents for managing the environments and compute that these agents are running in, for working with the artifacts that they produce.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All of that is exposed in an API that you can build on top of.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this ability to build on top of these primitives that are exposed via an API becomes really useful because anyone can build tools that overlap on top of these agentic experiences.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like interesting phenomena that's happened for us internally is we have a bunch of non-engineering teammates at Warp who have been able to use our SDK and API to build custom Slack bots to do a bunch of things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we have folks in our developer relations team who have actually built out tooling to help us manage all of our social mentions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So as tweets and Reddit posts and things are coming in, we have agents that will pick them up, do some sentiment analysis on them, try and understand what the user wants, and then propose a response that folks on our social media team should use in response to the original tweet or Reddit post or what have you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And all of this is enabled by our SDK.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you see a plethora of these types of experiences internally at Warp.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have people who have used them to help answer queries about how our product is working, do competitive research, all sorts of interesting things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And these primitives became a really big deal for us specifically when we decided to go open source.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As I mentioned earlier, Warp started off as a terminal, but it grew into an agentic development environment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And about three months ago, we decided to go open source.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This was much anticipated, long-awaited.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It was a huge success for us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The number of GitHub stars that we had, I think, catapulted from around 20,000 to over 60,000.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We had thousands of PRs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'll talk a little bit more about how we've been managing that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And hundreds of contributors who had been long-time users of the platform and were finally getting a chance to build on top of it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when we went open source, we wanted to be really thoughtful about how we could use agents to help us manage the repository.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We didn't want this to be the kind of thing where agents are just writing code and firing off PRs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We wanted them to participate kind of meaningfully in the structure that we used to triage issues that came into the repo, provide context around them, do implementation, do reviews.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But still have the space for humans to participate in this loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we did that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if you go to the warp open source repo right now, you'll notice that if you file a new issue with a bug report or a feature request, an agent will kick in and start to triage the issue automatically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It'll do research across the code base and context in the repo to understand what you're trying to propose.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It might ask you questions if it feels like your original query was a little abstract to get more information.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it will kind of do the work that's historically been very hard for open source, which is somebody has a problem or a bug that they want fixed, they don't give you enough details, and it's hard to get to the clarity that you need to get to to drive the work forward.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we can use agents to help us meaningfully in that way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They can also help draft initial specifications and work for tasks, do implementation, and provide a review gate.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So all PRs that get contributed to warp go through an agent-managed review process.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it goes through multiple iterations and we don't actually ping any of the human reviewers on our team until an agent has approved our PRs, which helps manage the workload a lot for the team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So all of those thousands of PRs, the things that humans actually have to manage are only the high-signal, high-quality ones.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And one of the key principles is that we improve the agent as we get more PRs in the repo and we see more examples of code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One of the things that we believe is that self-improvement loops are a really important way for you to enhance the overall SDLC life cycle that you're seeing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we did this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we had a light bulb moment because it unlocked something huge.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We had this structured process that could accommodate a big influx of issues and PRs on the repo.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the agents were there to support anyone in bringing their idea or their bug feature request or bug report to AWARP and then getting it through to the actual product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That key insight of agents providing structure and context was a really big thing for us because it meant that anyone could participate in translating their intent into implementation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And oftentimes the people who have really interesting intents and goals are the ones who are using software in interesting ways.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's not always the person that's building it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's the person who's kind of got domain knowledge in the space.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we're lucky because we're developers building a developer tool and that's a really unique niche to fill in.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But most software is developers building tools for non-developers in situations where they don't have domain expertise.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If we provide these structures and guardrails, though, people who are non-developers can have the necessary tools to ship serious software because the infrastructure to support them exists.
